overview: This label covers early medieval communities in Bohemia from 700 to 900, before the later Czech kingdom. It should not be read as a single state with fixed borders throughout those centuries. Settlements, workshops and changing strongholds reveal how local society developed as Přemyslid centres rose in importance.

periods.title: Villages and early strongholds
periods.summary: Eighth-century houses and fortified centres preserve different parts of regional life.

periods.title: Craft centres and princely foundations
periods.summary: Ninth-century centres combined skilled production, exchange and new Christian institutions.

sections.title: Homes and the work of living

items.text: At Březno near Louny, the eighth-century settlement had eight or nine partly sunken houses built over time, closer to the Ohře river than earlier dwellings. Ninth-century homes were more varied, including buildings with floors at ground level. A village could change its layout and building habits across generations.

How much space did a family need? In 1984, five people lived for thirteen days in a reconstruction of a ninth-century Březno house. This modern experiment tested the room available for daily tasks; it does not tell us the precise size of an original household.

Separate winter experiments at Březno found that smoke could form a layer about 1.2 to 1.5 metres above the floor. Working lower down helped avoid it. The result makes household heating surprisingly tangible, while remaining a finding from reconstructed houses rather than a measurement inside every medieval home.

Doubravčice became an eighth-century fortified centre on a site already used in prehistory. Its surviving banks belong to different periods, while some smaller ridges are probably later field boundaries. Archaeologists must sort these layers before drawing a picture of the early medieval settlement.

At Tismice, radiocarbon evidence places several phases of settlement and fortification between the last third of the eighth century and the end of the ninth. Geophysical survey and small excavation trenches help researchers investigate a large site without digging up its entire surface.

The Tismice study examined about 170 ornaments made from non-ferrous metals, mainly belt and horse-harness fittings. Gilded pieces and spurs suggest that some residents displayed wealth and status through clothing and riding equipment. Even a horse could arrive dressed for an important occasion.

Ingots and unfinished objects show that Tismice craftspeople made things locally, as well as receiving imported goods. Evidence of working gold was recovered in the 2018 excavation. The incomplete pieces are especially useful: they preserve stages of manufacture that a finished ornament would hide.

Šárka, above a stream valley in what is now Prague, was probably founded in the eighth century. Avar-period cast fittings and Frankish coins indicate distant connections among its elite. Researchers therefore interpret it as a centre for administration and exchange as well as defence.

sections.title: New centres and words on a coin

items.text: At Levý Hradec, occupation around the middle of the ninth century was followed by timber-and-earth defences faced with stone. Prince Bořivoj had a church dedicated to St Clement built there in the 880s. The changing enclosure and religious building show investment in a princely centre.

Budeč developed in the late ninth or perhaps early tenth century, around the edge of this map interval. Its complex included a palisaded princely residence and the rotunda of Saints Peter and Paul, still standing today. The stone church was only one part of a much larger settlement.

Excavations at Prague Castle uncovered the late-ninth-century Church of the Virgin Mary. Its surviving traces include masonry, pieces of a limestone-tile floor and the altar foundations. These modest remains belong to the early Christian centre, centuries before the enormous cathedral familiar today.

A silver coin found at Tismice in 2011 carries “CARO / LVS”, meaning “Charles”. The slash marks its two lines. Scholars identify it as a Charlemagne denier from Amiens, minted in 771 to 793/794. These are Latin letters on an imported object, not a surviving sentence in early Czech.

ending.text: The year 900 is a map boundary, not the end of the Czech people. Regional power increasingly centred on Přemyslid strongholds, while places such as Šárka lost importance. Communities and settlement traditions continued within the developing Bohemian polity.
